title: Projective-space immersion of an affine homogeneous quotient
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Group schemes and homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme], closed subgroups as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], finite type as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and smoothness and connectedness as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Let $G$ be smooth and affine of finite type over $k$, let $H\hookrightarrow G$ be any closed subgroup, and suppose $q:G\to Y$ is a quotient with $Y$ a separated finite-type $k$-scheme [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-proper-morphism]. By a quotient here we mean that $q$ is faithfully flat and of finite presentation, is invariant under right multiplication by $H$, and that $(g,h)\mapsto(g,gh)$ is an isomorphism $G\times_kH\simeq G\times_YG$; faithfully flat means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] and surjective, and finite presentation means locally of finite presentation [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], quasi-compact and quasi-separated [def-weil-quasi-separated-morphism]. Products are fibre products [def-pc-fibre-product]. Then there exist $N\geq0$ and a $k$-immersion $j:Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_k$, where immersion means a closed immersion into an open subscheme [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-weil-open-immersion], and $\mathbf P^N_k$ is projective space [def-nagata-projective-space-base-change]. No normality or smoothness of $H$, connectedness or reductivity of $G$, or perfection of $k$ is assumed. The case $H=G$, including $G=1$, is allowed.

source.place: Theorem 7.18 and its proof, printed p.143, using Theorem 4.27, printed pp.94--95, and Proposition 7.17, printed p.143. Also Theorem 8.43, printed p.161. Only quasi-projectivity is asserted, not properness.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-chevalley-scheme-line-stabilizer] to the affine finite-type $k$-group $G$ and its closed subgroup $H$. Obtain a nonzero representation $E$, a line $D\subseteq E$, and equality $H(A)=\{g:\rho_A(g)D_A=D_A\}$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. Choose a basis of $E$ and put $N=\dim_k(E)-1\geq0$. The equality is scheme-theoretic, so it retains infinitesimal stabilizers.

source.place: Theorem 7.18, first sentence; Theorem 4.27 and Remark 4.30, pp.94--96,143.

proof.text: Use [lem-weil-pbc-projective-space-functor-of-points] and base change to $k$ (a $k$-morphism $T\to\mathbf P^N_k=\operatorname{Spec}k\times_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf P^N_{\mathbf Z}$ is a morphism $T\to\mathbf P^N_{\mathbf Z}$ by [def-pc-fibre-product]) to interpret $\mathbf P^N_k(T)$ as locally direct-summand line subbundles $L\subseteq E\otimes_k\mathcal O_T$: send $L$ to the invertible quotient $E^*\otimes\mathcal O_T\twoheadrightarrow L^*$ with the sections from the dual basis, and recover $L$ by dualizing that quotient. These operations are inverse on a local basis and commute with pullback. Thus $g\cdot L=\rho_T(g)L$ is a natural transformation on test schemes. Yoneda [lem-pc-yoneda] makes it a morphism $G\times_k\mathbf P^N_k\to\mathbf P^N_k$; its unit and multiplication identities follow on test schemes from those for $\rho$. The constant line $D$ defines $x\in\mathbf P^N_k(k)$, and the stabilizer of $x$ on every $A$ is precisely $H(A)$ by step 1. This extends to every $k$-scheme $T$: whether $g\in G(T)$ factors through the closed subscheme $H$, and whether $\rho_T(g)$ fixes $D\otimes\mathcal O_T$, are both checked on an affine open cover of $T$. In particular the orbit map $b(g)=gD$ satisfies $b(gh)=b(g)$.

source.place: Theorem 7.18, projective-space functor and induced action, p.143; Stacks Tag 01NE (lemma-projective-space).

proof.text: Projective space is proper over $k$ by [lemma-nagata-projective-space-base-change-proper], hence separated and finite type by [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-rational-orbit-arbitrary-field] to this action at $x$: it gives an immersion $i:O\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_k$ and $b=i\circ\beta$ with $\beta:G\to O$ flat, surjective and locally of finite presentation. Its hypotheses use the smoothness of $G$ and impose no smoothness on $H$.

source.place: Theorem 7.18, last sentence, using Proposition 7.17 and Proposition 7.4(b), pp.139--140,143.

proof.text: The two kernel pairs are the same right-$H$ relation. For $\beta$ the inverse to $(g,h)\mapsto(g,gh)$ is $(g,g')\mapsto(g,g^{-1}g')$: equality $\beta(g)=\beta(g')$ is equivalent to $gD=g'D$, since $i$ is an immersion and thus injective on test-scheme morphisms. It is equivalent to $g^{-1}g'$ stabilizing $D$, namely belonging to $H$, by steps 1--2. The formulas are natural on test schemes, and the group identities show they are inverse. Hence the fibre-product universal property [def-pc-fibre-product] and Yoneda [lem-pc-yoneda] give $G\times_O G\simeq G\times_kH$ with projections $(g,h)\mapsto g,gh$. Here test-scheme injectivity of $i$ follows directly from its open/closed factorization: both inclusions are monomorphisms (locally, the closed inclusion is a quotient of rings). The given quotient hypothesis already supplies the identical description of $G\times_YG$.

source.place: Proposition 7.11 and proof, pp.141--142; Theorem 7.18, stabilizer identification, p.143.

proof.text: Both $q$ and $\beta$ are singleton fppf coverings by [def-pc-fppf-site]: they are flat, surjective and locally of finite presentation. They are fpqc coverings by [lem-trf-fppf-covering-is-fpqc]. Since $\beta(gh)=\beta(g)$, [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] descends $\beta$ along $q$ to $u:Y\to O$ with $u q=\beta$. The equality of the kernel pairs in step 4 and $q(gh)=q(g)$ descend $q$ along $\beta$ to $v:O\to Y$ with $v\beta=q$. Now $(vu)q=q$ and $(uv)\beta=\beta$; uniqueness in the same descent statement gives $vu=\mathrm{id}_Y$ and $uv=\mathrm{id}_O$. The descended maps are over $k$, since their composites to $\operatorname{Spec}k$ agree after their fpqc covers, where that uniqueness applies again. Thus $u$ is a $k$-isomorphism.

source.place: Propositions 7.11--7.12, pp.141--142, quotient identification; explicit uniqueness via Stacks Tag 023Q (lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms) and Tag 022C.

proof.text: Set $j=i\circ u$. Write the immersion $i$ as $O\hookrightarrow U\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_k$ with the first arrow closed and the second open. Precomposing the first arrow with the isomorphism $u$ preserves its closed image and the surjective map of structure sheaves, so [def-weil-closed-immersion] makes $Y\to U$ a closed immersion. Therefore $j$ is the required $k$-immersion. When $H=G$, Chevalley's line is $G$-stable and its orbit is the rational point $x$; the same descent gives $Y\simeq\operatorname{Spec}k$, so this case (including $G=1$) is included.

source.place: Theorem 7.18 and Example 7.19, p.143; definition of immersion.
